summary: Defines the Remote Direct Memory Access Protocol, which runs over DDP and offers read and write services so data goes directly into application buffers without extra copies. It allows kernel bypass. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Lets one computer put data into another's memory directly, without extra handing around.

questions: what is an stag in rdma
subtitle: How one computer reads and writes another's memory directly, without extra copies or CPU work.

tldr.problem: Communication over TCP/IP typically needs copy operations, which add latency and use significant CPU and memory resources.
tldr.mechanism: RDMAP sits on top of the Direct Data Placement protocol (DDP) and defines seven operations: Send variants, RDMA Write, RDMA Read and Terminate. Data lands directly in buffers the remote side has advertised with a Steering Tag.
tldr.outcome: RDMAP is the top layer of the iWARP suite and is a Proposed Standard. RFC 7146 updates it.

facts.label: Read Request Header fields
facts.value: Two 32-bit STags, two 64-bit offsets, one 32-bit size

today: RFC 5040 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 7146; it has not been obsoleted. It defines the RDMAP layer that sits on DDP (RFC 5041).

sections.title: Goals and Layering
sections.content:
Communication over TCP/IP typically needs copy operations that add latency and consume CPU and memory. The Remote Direct Memory Access Protocol (RDMAP) lets a local application read or write data in a remote computer's memory with minimal demand on memory bus bandwidth and CPU, while keeping memory protection. It also allows a kernel bypass implementation.

RDMAP is layered on Direct Data Placement (DDP, see RFC 5041) and uses both of its buffer models. DDP in turn runs over MPA and TCP (RFC 5044), or over SCTP. The combination of RDMAP, DDP and MPA is called iWARP. A single RDMA Write, Read or Send can move up to 2^32 - 1 octets, and all operations on one RDMAP Stream are transmitted reliably in the order submitted.
sections.plainLanguage: RDMAP is the top layer of a stack of helpers. Its job is to let one machine put data into another machine's memory without lots of copying along the way.

sections.title: Buffers, Tags and Placement
sections.content:
A Tagged Buffer is a region of memory that has been advertised to the remote side by giving it an STag (Steering Tag), a Tagged Offset and a length. How the advertisement travels is left to the upper layer protocol (ULP); a typical way is to embed the details in a Send message. An Untagged Buffer is not advertised and is used for control-style messages: Send, RDMA Read Request and Terminate.

The RFC separates Placement (writing data into a buffer, which may happen in any order) from Delivery (telling the ULP a message is available, whose order is strictly defined). RDMAP uses three DDP queues for Untagged Buffers: queue 0 for Send operations, queue 1 for RDMA Read Requests and queue 2 for Terminate.
sections.plainLanguage: A tagged buffer is a shelf with a labelled address you have shared with a friend, so they can put things on it directly. An untagged buffer is the mailbox where you receive ordinary notes.

sections.title: The Seven Operations
sections.content:
RDMAP provides seven operations. Except for RDMA Read, each generates exactly one RDMA Message.

  • Send, Send with Invalidate, Send with Solicited Event (SE) and Send with SE and Invalidate put data into an Untagged Buffer that was not advertised. The Invalidate forms carry an STag that can no longer be accessed remotely afterwards. The SE forms may raise an Event at the receiver if it is configured to generate one.
  • RDMA Write places data into a previously advertised Tagged Buffer. A valid Write is placed by DDP and MUST NOT be delivered to the receiving ULP, so a later Send is the usual way to signal it. One Write can target only one remote Tagged Buffer.
  • RDMA Read pulls data from the remote side. It is a single Read Request (untagged, sent to queue 1) answered by a single Read Response (tagged), with no ULP involvement at the data source.
  • Terminate reports an error and ends the stream.

Sends consume one Untagged Buffer each. A Send larger than the receiver's buffer is an error.
sections.plainLanguage: You can hand someone a note (Send), put something on their labelled shelf (Write), fetch something from their labelled shelf (Read), or shout that something went wrong and stop (Terminate).

sections.title: Headers and Opcodes
sections.content:
RDMAP has almost no header of its own. It uses the first octet that DDP reserves for upper layers as the RDMAP Control Field, which holds the RDMA version and a 4-bit opcode. Version 01b is for RNICs that follow this specification and 00b for the RDMA Consortium's earlier specification; both are valid. For the two Invalidate Sends, the next four octets carry the STag to invalidate. RDMAP does not need a length field because DDP provides the message length.

Only two messages carry an RDMAP header. The RDMA Read Request Header describes both buffers: the Data Sink STag (32 bits) and Tagged Offset (64 bits), the RDMA Read Message Size (32 bits), and the Data Source STag (32 bits) and Tagged Offset (64 bits). One request can read from 0 to 2^32-1 octets. The Terminate Header carries a Terminate Control field (layer, error type, error code and header-control bits) and, when relevant, the offending DDP and RDMA headers.
sections.plainLanguage: The label on each parcel says what kind of parcel it is. Only the two special kinds, a request to fetch something and an error report, need an extra form attached.

sections.title: Ordering, Streams and Errors
sections.content:
Ordering rules matter because data may be placed out of order. RDMAP gives no ordering across different RDMAP Streams or between operations generated at the two ends of one stream. Buffer contents may be indeterminate until the matching Send or Read Response is delivered, so the RFC warns against "peeking" at data to see if it has arrived. Sends and Read Responses MUST be delivered to the ULP in order, and operations complete at the local peer in the order submitted.

A Read Response may reflect a later Write to the same buffer. If that is not wanted, the ULP must fence the later Write until outstanding Read Responses are delivered. The ULP negotiates the maximum number of outstanding RDMA Read Requests per stream direction, and RDMAP MUST NOT exceed it.

RDMAP has no built-in error recovery. On an RDMAP or DDP error it sends a Terminate message and tears the stream down, which the RFC considers far simpler than trying to continue when the cause is unknown. After sending a Terminate, a peer MUST NOT send more messages on that stream, and the state of outstanding messages is indeterminate.
sections.plainLanguage: Boxes can arrive on shelves in any order, so you must wait for the "all delivered" note before looking. If something goes badly wrong, the system stops the whole delivery and says why instead of guessing how to fix it.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
Because RDMAP lets a remote peer touch local memory, the RFC lists firm rules for the RNIC (the RDMA-capable network adapter). Examples: a stream in one Protection Domain MUST NOT access an STag in another; a remote peer MUST NOT reach memory outside the buffer enabled for it; and STag values MUST be difficult to predict, with sparse population over the available range RECOMMENDED. A Privileged Resource Manager must control allocation of scarce resources such as completion queue entries. A detailed analysis lives in RFC 5042.

Since all packets are exposed to spoofing, tampering and disclosure, the RFC points to IPsec. RDMAP can run over IPsec without change, and implementations MUST meet the IPsec requirements of RFC 3723, including ESP with replay protection. SSL or TLS is described as less appropriate, and SSL layered on top of RDMAP would not protect the RDMAP headers.
sections.plainLanguage: Letting a stranger's machine write into your memory is risky, so each shelf gets a hard-to-guess label and strict limits, and the delivery route can be locked with encryption.

messages.label: RDMA Read Request
messages.note: Untagged; gives the STag, offset and length of both buffers to the Read Request Queue.

messages.label: RDMA Read Response
messages.note: Tagged; fills the Data Sink buffer without involving the source ULP.

items.label: RDMA Read Request
items.desc: Untagged, queue 1; carries the Read Request Header.

items.label: Send with Invalidate
items.desc: Untagged, queue 0; carries an Invalidate STag.

items.label: Send with SE
items.desc: Untagged, queue 0; may raise an Event.

items.label: Send with SE and Invalidate
items.desc: Untagged, queue 0; Event and Invalidate STag.

items.label: Terminate
items.desc: Untagged, queue 2; carries the Terminate Header.

fields.name: Data Sink STag
fields.desc: Identifies the Data Sink's Tagged Buffer; copied into the Read Response.

fields.name: Data Sink Tagged Offset
fields.desc: Starting offset in the sink buffer where data is written.

fields.name: Data Source STag
fields.desc: Identifies the Data Source's Tagged Buffer.

fields.name: Data Source Tagged Offset
fields.desc: Starting offset to read from in the source buffer.
